title: Flue gas inert gas system
plain: Do the officers know how the flue gas inert gas plant works, and is it run and maintained to the maker's instructions?
why: A weak inert gas plant can send air or bad gas into cargo tanks, which risks fire and explosion.
checks: Company procedures for operating, inspecting, testing and maintaining the plant
Machinery space plant: leaks, pinholes, temporary repairs, vibration
Gas regulating valve and remote isolation valves working automatically or remotely
Temperature and pressure sensors connected and showing sensible values
Safe entry procedure posted if the plant is in an enclosed room
ready: Procedures covering boiler uptake valves, scrubber, demister, blowers and gas regulating valve
Manufacturer's instruction and maintenance manual
Record of inspection, testing and maintenance, with defects and how they were fixed
Planned maintenance records showing jobs done on time
Enclosed space entry notice at each entrance of the IG room
traps: No procedure covering all five main parts of the plant
Officer cannot explain how the plant is operated, inspected and tested
Gas regulating valve or remote valves running on local control
Sensors disconnected or defective
Gas or liquid leaks, or blower shaking badly
Records missing or incomplete
Posted entry rules do not match the SMS enclosed space procedure
say: Our SMS has a procedure for running, inspecting, testing and maintaining the flue gas plant, including the uptake valves, scrubber, demister, blowers and gas regulating valve. I can show you the maker's manual and our inspection and maintenance records, including defects and how we fixed them. Deck and engine departments work together on this plant.

practice.q: What are the main parts of your flue gas inert gas plant?
a: Boiler uptake valves
Scrubber and demister
Blowers
Gas regulating valve

practice.q: Where do I find proof that the plant is in good working order?
a: Inspection and maintenance records
Defects and their rectification recorded
Planned maintenance history

tip: Walk the IG room before the inspection and look for small leaks, temporary patches and valves left in local mode.

title: Cargo tank high level and overfill alarms
plain: Do the officers know how to maintain, test and set the high-level and high-high-level alarms, and do they all work and sit at the right settings?
why: These alarms are the last warning before a tank overflows, which means pollution and fire risk.
checks: Company procedure for maintenance, setting and testing of both alarms
Alarm panel in the cargo control room: switched on, all tanks monitored
Audible and visible alarms in the control room and on deck
Test of a high-high alarm on a tank the inspector picks at random
Your knowledge of when alarms may be isolated and the safeguards
ready: Procedure with set points, test method and test frequency
Testing and maintenance records
Rules on use of automatic closing valves, if fitted
Risk-assessment-based procedure for loading on if an alarm fails
Panels and alarm units clearly labelled as high level or high-high level
traps: High-level and high-high alarms not independent of each other
High-high alarm not independent of the fixed gauging system
High-level set at or above the high-high point
High-high set too late to stop transfer before overflow, typically 98 percent
Alarms silenced, inhibited or not working in the control room or on deck
Alarms not tested to the manufacturer's instructions
Chemical ship: high-level alarm tied to the gauging system, or auto closing valves used without approval
say: Our SMS requires both alarms to be in use for every loading, discharge and transfer. Set points, test method, test frequency and records are all in our procedure. I can show you the test records and demonstrate a high-high alarm on any tank you choose. Any isolation follows the risk-assessed procedure.

practice.q: When can a tank alarm be isolated, and what protects you then?
a: Only as the company procedure allows
Risk assessment-based safeguards in place
Alarms otherwise always in use during transfers

practice.q: At what level are your high and high-high alarms set?
a: Read the set points from the procedure
High-level typically 95 percent
High-high typically 98 percent, early enough to stop transfer

tip: Test all alarms before cargo ops and write the test in the record the same day, so the paper matches the practice.

title: Gauging and sampling static accumulator cargo in non-inerted tanks
plain: Do crew know and follow the extra static electricity precautions when dipping, ullaging and sampling in non-inerted tanks?
why: A static charge on the cargo can spark and ignite flammable vapour inside the tank.
checks: Company procedure for dipping, ullaging and sampling in non-inerted tanks
Equipment used, and how it is bonded, earthed and cleaned
Settling time observed after loading before gauging
Sounding pipe type and information displayed at the cargo control position
Cargo logs and records, and observation of gauging if possible
ready: Procedure covering equipment, bonding, earthing, cleaning and settling time
Plan for fixed gauging failure if fitted but no inert gas or full-depth sounding pipes
Drawings or plans of the tank sounding pipes
Cargo log books and records
No synthetic ropes or tapes for lowering equipment; natural fibre rope for sample holders
traps: No information on sounding pipe type at the control position
Metal gauging or sampling gear put in tank during loading or within 30 minutes after, without a full-length sounding pipe
Plastic sample container over one litre used in the same time window
Synthetic rope or tape used to lower equipment
Non-metal sample bottle rubbed dry before use
Metal parts of equipment not bonded to the ship
Sounding pipe not metal, not full depth or not bonded and earthed
say: Our procedure says what equipment we use, how it is bonded and earthed, and that we wait 30 minutes after loading before using metal gear unless we use a full-depth sounding pipe. We never use synthetic ropes or tapes. Our records show we follow this, and the sounding pipe details are displayed at the cargo control position.

practice.q: How long do you wait after loading before using metal gauging gear in a non-inerted tank?
a: 30 minutes settling time
Bond and earth before it enters the tank
Keep earthed until it is out

practice.q: What rope do you use to lower sampling equipment?
a: Natural fibre rope
Never synthetic ropes or tapes
Do not rub non-metal bottles dry

tip: Ratings do the actual dipping, so brief the deck gang with this checklist at the pre-cargo toolbox talk.

title: Loading static accumulator cargo into non-inerted tanks
plain: Do officers know and follow the company procedure for loading static accumulator cargo into non-inerted tanks?
why: Fast or splashing loading builds up static charge, which can ignite flammable vapour in the tank.
checks: Company procedure for identifying static accumulator cargoes and loading precautions
Initial and bulk loading rates in cargo plans and logs
Bottom entry loading, no free fall, no splashing
Whether lines were blown with compressed air after loading
Your knowledge of the procedure, and loading observed if possible
ready: Procedure covering water hazard, initial rate, bulk rate, spread loading, switch loading, additives, filters
Cargo plans and cargo log books
List or table of which cargoes are static accumulators
Loading rate records at each tank inlet
Procedure for loading into uncleaned tanks that held a more volatile cargo
traps: No procedure for spotting static accumulator cargoes
Initial rate over 1 m/s at the tank inlet
Initial slow rate held for too short a time
Bulk rate over 1 m/s when the cargo is not clean
Loading over the top or splash filling
Lines blown with compressed air after loading
Low volatility cargo into an uncleaned tank that held a high volatility cargo, without precautions
say: Our procedure tells us how to identify static accumulators and what to do when loading them into non-inerted tanks. We start at no more than 1 metre per second at the tank inlet and keep it there for the required time, load by bottom entry and do not blow lines with air. The logs show we follow it.

practice.q: What is your starting rate for a static accumulator in a non-inerted tank?
a: Maximum 1 m/s at each tank inlet
For 30 minutes or two pipeline volumes, whichever is less
Must also cover the fill pipe to twice its diameter

practice.q: When can you go above 1 m/s later in the load?
a: Only if the product is clean
Less than 0.5 percent free water
Less than 10 mg/l suspended solids

tip: If you are in doubt whether a product is a static accumulator, treat it as one, as the guidance says.

title: Inert gas system oxygen analyser
plain: Do officers know how the fixed IG oxygen analyser works and is calibrated, and has it been calibrated and maintained correctly?
why: If the analyser reads wrong you could send gas with too much oxygen into the cargo tanks.
checks: Procedure for operation, testing and calibration of the fixed analyser
Analyser itself, with zero and span calibration arrangements
Local reading compared with cargo control room and engine control room readings
Calibration records showing calibration within 24 hours before each IG start
Clear instructions for use and calibration near the analyser
ready: Procedure including calibration method, frequency and action if the analyser fails
Manufacturer's manual
Calibration records for every cargo, purging or inerting operation
Suitable, in-date zero and span gas available
Inspection and maintenance records for the IG plant
traps: Not calibrated within 24 hours before starting the IG for each operation
Zero or span gas unsuitable, out of date or missing
No clear instructions beside the analyser
Officer cannot explain calibration method or what to do on failure
Local and remote readings do not agree
Records missing or incomplete
say: We calibrate the fixed oxygen analyser within 24 hours before starting the inert gas plant for each cargo, purging or inerting job, using in-date zero and span gas. The record is kept and instructions are posted at the analyser. If it fails, we follow our procedure for failure of the analyser.

practice.q: How soon before starting IG must the analyser be calibrated?
a: Not more than 24 hours before
Every cargo, purging or inerting operation
Recorded in the calibration log

practice.q: What do you do if the fixed analyser fails?
a: Follow the company failure procedure
Use the portable analyser as procedure allows
Report and repair, record the defect

tip: Check the date on the calibration gas bottles every time you do the analyser calibration, not just when the inspector comes.

title: ESD and cargo pump emergency stop controls
plain: Do officers and ratings know the ESD system and cargo pump emergency stops, and has everything been tested as the company procedure requires?
why: In an emergency the cargo system must be stopped quickly and safely to prevent spills and fire.
checks: Procedure for operating and testing ESD and pump emergency stops
Latest test records: ESD, automatic pump shutdown, each emergency stop location, each pump before use
Emergency stop controls clearly marked, reachable and ready
Which alarm conditions cause a pump to stop automatically
Deck rating questions: where the stops are and what to do after
ready: Procedure covering ESD, auto pump shutdown and emergency stops
Test records for each system and each pump before every cargo operation
ESD plan and signal agreed with the terminal
Clear access to every emergency stop, no obstructions
Crew familiarisation records for shutdown controls
traps: No procedure describing testing and operation
Tests not done as the company procedure requires
System defective in any way
Manual ESD or pump stop not clearly marked or ready for immediate use
Access to a stop control blocked
Officer unfamiliar with what alarms trip a pump automatically
Rating does not know stop locations, when to use them or what to do after
say: Our procedure covers the ESD, the automatic pump shutdowns and the manual emergency stops, including testing before each cargo operation. I can show you the test records and the stop locations. Crew know when to hit the stop and that closing a manifold valve against the flow is dangerous.

practice.q: When would you press the cargo pump emergency stop?
a: Spill, fire or abnormal condition
As the agreed ESD plan and procedure say
Then follow the actions in the procedure

practice.q: Why not shut a manifold valve against the flow?
a: Risk of pressure surge
Flow must be stopped by the pumps, ship or shore, as agreed in the ESD procedure
Follow the agreed ESD procedure

tip: Ask every deck rating on watch to show you where each pump stop is. If they hesitate, run a quick drill.

title: Pressure testing and inspection of cargo, inert gas and vapour pipelines
plain: Do officers know the company rules for inspecting and testing cargo, vapour and IG pipelines, and are the records available?
why: Hidden weak points in pipelines can leak cargo when the system is under pressure.
checks: Company procedure for inspection and testing of all three pipeline types
MAWP of the cargo transfer system determined and documented
Records: annual hydrostatic test at 100 percent MAWP, and 150 percent MAWP at least twice in any five years
Physical condition of pipelines, flanges, couplings, U-bolts
Your knowledge of how and when the last test was done
ready: Procedure with inspection frequency, test frequency and retest after repairs
MAWP calculation consistent with drawings and pump curves
Hydrostatic test records, including crude oil washing line if fitted
Pipelines marked with date and pressure of the last test
Inspection records for cargo, vapour and IG lines
traps: MAWP not determined or does not match drawings and pump curves
No hydrostatic test to 100 percent MAWP in the last 12 months
No 150 percent MAWP test at least twice in five years
Test done with compressed air or inert gas
Repairs or section replacement not retested
Pipelines not marked with date and pressure of last test
Visible poor condition not matching what the records say
say: Our procedure sets inspection frequencies, annual hydrostatic tests at 100 percent MAWP and 150 percent MAWP at least twice in five years, and retesting after repairs. The MAWP is documented. Lines are marked with the last test date and pressure, and I can show you the records.

practice.q: How do you work out the MAWP of the cargo system?
a: Relief valve setting, if fitted
Otherwise maximum pump discharge pressure
Centrifugal pump: pressure at zero flow

practice.q: Can you test the lines with compressed air?
a: No, must be a hydrostatic test
Air or inert gas is not acceptable
Retest after repairs or modifications

tip: Mark each cargo line with the date and pressure of the last test after every test. Unmarked lines are a negative finding.

title: Vapour collection system
plain: Do officers know the company procedures for inspecting, testing and running the vapour collection system, and is the equipment in good condition?
why: Wrong operation can over or under pressurise tanks or release toxic and flammable vapour.
checks: Company procedure and vapour collection system manual
Line diagram, relief settings, maximum transfer rate, pressure drop and pre-transfer tests
Main line pressure sensor with high and low pressure alarms at the cargo control room
Deck condition of the system and any vapour hoses on chemical ships
Training or familiarisation records for people in charge of transfer
ready: Procedure covering all items in the vapour system manual
Approval of the system by flag State or class
Records and checklists from the last time it was used
Training records for the person in charge
Maintenance and test records for vapour hoses on chemical tankers
traps: Procedure missing line diagram, transfer rates, pressure drop, relief settings or fault actions
Pressure sensor on the main vapour line not working
High or low pressure alarms defective or not set as procedure says
No evidence of training for the person in charge of transfer
Vapour system not approved by flag State or class
Vapour hoses on chemical tanker without maintenance and testing evidence
say: Our procedure covers the vapour line diagram, initial and maximum transfer rates, pressure drop, relief settings, pre-transfer tests and what to do on a fault. High and low pressure alarms work in the cargo control room. Persons in charge have been trained on our system.

practice.q: What tests do you do before using the vapour system?
a: P/V valves
Tank level gauges and alarms
High and low pressure alarms

practice.q: What if something goes wrong during vapour return?
a: Follow the fault procedure
Stop or reduce the transfer as procedure says
Inform the terminal

tip: Keep the vapour system manual next to the cargo control room copy of the procedures so it is found in seconds.

title: Tank cleaning in non-inert tanks
plain: Do officers and ratings know and follow the company procedure for washing tanks in a non-inert atmosphere after volatile cargo?
why: Washing creates static charge, so the tank atmosphere and ignition sources must both be controlled.
checks: Company procedure for non-inert tank washing after volatile cargo
Tank cleaning plans, risk assessments, logs and records
Electrical continuity test records for portable hoses and connections
Fixed and portable washing equipment condition and identification marking
Rating's knowledge of putting sounding rods and equipment into a tank during washing
ready: Procedure covering fuel and ignition control, bonding, hose testing, free fall, no steaming
Completed tank cleaning plans and risk assessments
Hose continuity test records, not more than 6 ohms per metre
Hoses indelibly marked for identification
Gas readings taken frequently at several levels
traps: Tank bottom or lines not flushed and stripped before washing
Atmosphere not ventilated to 10 percent LFL or below before washing
Washing continued above 35 percent LFL, or restarted above 10 percent
Wash water over the recommended throughput, or recirculated water used
Steam injected into a tank not gas free
Hoses not tested, not marked, or over 6 ohms per metre
Slop tank liquid not at least 1 metre above the inlets
say: Our procedure controls the gas and the ignition sources. We flush and strip first, ventilate to 10 percent LFL or less, stop at 35 percent LFL, test hoses for continuity and never use recirculated water or steam. Records and equipment are available to show.

practice.q: At what gas level do you stop washing?
a: 35 percent LFL anywhere in the tank
Resume only at 10 percent LFL or less
Keep ventilating

practice.q: What do you check before using a portable washing hose?
a: Electrical continuity, dry hose
Not over 6 ohms per metre
Hose marked and test recorded

tip: Brief the deck rating on sounding gear rules before washing starts, because they are the ones asked by the inspector.

title: Portable UTI measurement and sampling equipment
plain: Do officers know the company procedures for portable UTI and sampling gear, and is it in good condition and used correctly?
why: Wrong or unbonded gauging gear can release vapour or cause a static spark.
checks: Company procedure for use, testing, calibration and servicing of portable UTI and sampling equipment
Service and calibration records and certificates for each unit
Two units tested: right rating, earth wire fixed, ullage and temperature work in a bucket of water
Control of who opens vapour locks and ullage ports
Rating's knowledge of earthing, PPE and RPE
ready: Procedure explaining closed, restricted and open measurement and when each is allowed
Manufacturer's manuals and pre-operation check records
Calibration certificates for every unit
Number of units onboard matching what the procedure requires
PPE and RPE ready for open gauging
traps: Equipment rating not suitable for the cargo, such as restricted gear where closed is required
Unit used without bonding in a non-inert tank
Vapour locks leaking, damaged, missing, or opened by unauthorised persons
Open tank openings left open after gauging
Service or calibration not done, or no certificate
Too few units: no fixed system and not enough units plus two spares
Officer or rating unaware of PPE, RPE or bonding rules
say: Our procedure explains closed, restricted and open gauging, the rating of each instrument, bonding, pre-use checks and PPE and RPE. All units are serviced and calibrated with certificates. Vapour locks are controlled, and tank openings are closed straight after use.

practice.q: Which type of gauging do you prefer, and why?
a: Closed gauging, full containment
Open or restricted only where regulations allow
Pressure relieved before use

practice.q: How do you check a UTI unit before use?
a: Earth wire and clip fitted
Test sensor in a bucket of water
Compare temperature with a thermometer

tip: Keep a bucket and a thermometer ready in the cargo control room so a quick UTI check can be shown any time.

title: Secondary venting systems
plain: Do officers know how the primary and secondary tank venting systems work under SOLAS, and are they set correctly?
why: If the main vent fails or is closed by mistake, the secondary protection stops tanks bursting or collapsing.
checks: Company procedure for primary and secondary venting for each tank or tank group set-up
Venting arrangement compared with SOLAS and what the HVPQ says
Pressure and vacuum sensors working and alarms at correct settings, where fitted
Test and calibration records for the pressure sensors
Your knowledge of the required alarm settings
ready: Procedure with the primary and secondary system for each tank configuration
Ship's drawings of the venting arrangement
Cargo handling manual
Test and calibration records for tank pressure sensors
Alarm set points written down and known
traps: No procedure for primary and secondary venting for each tank set-up
Arrangement not as described in HVPQ or PIQ
Secondary means not meeting SOLAS full flow relief
Vapour isolating valves that can be damaged or closed by mistake, with no full-flow P/V valve or pressure monitoring
Chemical carrier with one P/V valve per tank and no secondary protection
Pressure sensors not working, inaccurate or alarms at wrong values
No sensor test or calibration records
say: Our procedure shows the primary and secondary venting for each tank arrangement and the alarm settings for the pressure and vacuum sensors. The sensors are tested and calibrated to the maker's instructions and I can show the records. Sensor alarms are set above the normal valve settings but always within tank design limits.

practice.q: What is your secondary protection against over or under pressure?
a: Second full-flow P/V valve or pressure sensors in each tank
Alarm monitored in the cargo control room
As described in the HVPQ

practice.q: Where are the pressure sensor alarms set?
a: 10 percent above the normal P/V valve settings, or per the flow diagrams on non-inerted ships
Never above tank design pressure
On inerted ships the low pressure alarm is set above zero

tip: Know the set points by heart and keep the venting drawing handy. Officers who guess here usually get caught.

title: Cargo tank venting systems
plain: Do officers know the company procedures for operating, inspecting, testing and maintaining the tank venting systems, and are they in good condition?
why: Severely over or under pressurised tanks have caused serious accidents on tankers.
checks: Company procedure for P/V valves, high velocity vents, mast risers, vent stacks, vacuum valves, flame screens, vapour lines
Records of inspection, maintenance and pre-operation tests
Maximum permissible loading rate for each tank or tank group
Physical condition on deck, including flame screens
High velocity vents operated correctly, not jacked open
ready: Procedure covering all venting components
P/V valve and high velocity vent records, maybe in planned maintenance
Ship shore safety checklists showing free movement check, Part 1A item 6
Maximum loading rate information for each tank or group
Clean, intact flame screens
traps: No inspection, test and maintenance records
P/V valves or vents not checked for free movement before each cargo operation
No maximum loading rate information available
Flame screen damaged, clogged or missing
P/V valve passing vapour or drawing air inside its set pressure or vacuum
High velocity vents jacked open during cargo operations
Vapour line heavily corroded or with soft patches
say: Our procedure covers every part of the venting system, and we check P/V valves and high velocity vents for free movement before each cargo operation, as the safety checklist requires. The maximum permissible loading rate for each tank or tank group is available. We never jack high velocity vents open.

practice.q: When do you check the P/V valves for free movement?
a: Before every cargo operation
Recorded on the ship shore checklist
Defects reported and repaired

practice.q: Why must you not jack a high velocity vent open?
a: It needs pressure build-up to open at set point
Gives the high exit velocity of at least 30 m/s
Jacking defeats its protection

tip: Look up at the mast risers and flame screens during your pre-inspection walk. Clogged screens are easy to miss from the deck.

title: Deepwell pump cofferdam purging
plain: Do officers know how to monitor leakage into deepwell pump cofferdams, and has regular purging been done to spot excessive leakage?
why: Purging shows if shaft seals are failing before cargo or hydraulic oil leaks into the cofferdam and the pump fails.
checks: Company procedure for monitoring cofferdam leakage
Purging records for each deepwell pump
Your knowledge of connections, controls and indicators used when purging
Maximum purge medium pressure and the medium required for recent cargoes
Pumpman's knowledge of safety precautions while purging
ready: Procedure covering purging, precautions, medium and pressure, frequency, records, acceptable leakage and actions
Manufacturer's instruction manual for the pumps
Detailed purging records with results reviewed
Defect reports for any pump with high leakage or a blocked cofferdam
PPE for the person purging
traps: No company procedure for monitoring leakage
Purging not done as the procedure says
No detailed records of purging
Leakage above manufacturer's limits but no defect report raised
Apparently blocked cofferdam but no defect report
Rating does not know the purging safety precautions
Officer unsure of the maximum purge pressure or correct purge medium
say: We purge the deepwell cofferdams on the frequency in our procedure, using the medium and maximum pressure in the maker's manual, with proper PPE. Results are recorded and compared with the manufacturer's limits, and any high leakage or blockage gets a defect report.

practice.q: Why do you purge the cofferdams?
a: Check shaft seals for leakage
Detect cargo, hydraulic or lube oil leaking in
Act early on abnormal results

practice.q: What are the safety precautions when purging?
a: Exhaust gas and liquid may be hazardous
Wear suitable PPE
Use the right medium and pressure limit

tip: Write the purge result as a number or description every time, not just a tick, so trends can be seen.

title: Inert gas system non-return devices
plain: Do officers know the purpose, operation, testing and maintenance of the IG non-return devices, and are they in good condition?
why: These devices stop cargo vapour or liquid flowing back into the engine room or other gas-safe spaces.
checks: Company procedure covering deck seal or double block and bleed, and the non-return valve
IG main non-return valve opened and inspected as the procedure requires
Deck seal: clear level gauge, correct water level, condition of seal and pipework
Double block and bleed valves operating automatically and tested for tightness
Records of inspection, testing and maintenance
ready: Procedure for the deck seal or block and bleed and non-return valve
Evidence the non-return valve was opened and inspected
Evidence the deck seal was opened and inspected, including pipework
Test records for block and bleed valves
IG plant inspection and maintenance record with defects and fixes
traps: No procedure including the deck seal or block and bleed and the non-return valve
No evidence non-return valve was opened and inspected
Deck seal level gauge not clear or readable
Deck seal water level not as required
Seal or pipework in poor condition
Block and bleed valves not operating automatically, or no test evidence
Device defective in any way
say: Our procedure covers the deck seal or block and bleed arrangement and the non-return valve. The non-return valve and deck seal have been opened and inspected as our procedure requires, and I can show the records. The level gauge is clear and the water level is correct.

practice.q: What is the purpose of the non-return devices?
a: Stop vapour and liquid returning to the IG plant
Protect engine room and gas-safe spaces
Two devices required, deck seal or block and bleed first

practice.q: How do you know the deck seal is working properly?
a: Clear gauge showing correct level
Inspection of seal and pipework
Opened and inspected as per procedure

tip: If your ship has a dry type deck seal, be ready to explain it, because the inspector notes it in the report.

title: Manifold reducers and spool pieces
plain: Do officers know the company rules for using, inspecting and testing reducers, spool pieces and portable pipework, and are they in good condition and fitted correctly?
why: Under-rated or damaged reducers can leak at the flange face during cargo transfer.
checks: Company procedure covering use, certificates, storage, inspection and testing
Inventory of reducers, spool pieces and other portable pipework
Test certificates and records, including annual pressure testing
Flange faces of a stored reducer, with covers removed
Fitted arrangement: only one reducer or spool piece, supported if long
ready: Procedure with correct use, certification, storage, inspection and annual pressure test
Complete inventory
Pressure test certificates showing same or higher rating than fixed manifold
Each item marked with date and pressure of last test
Flange face covers fitted in storage
traps: No inventory or test certificate for an item
Not pressure tested to 100 percent MAWP in the last 12 months
Not marked with date and pressure of last test
Rating lower than the fixed manifold piping
Lifting lugs or handles interfering with couplers or bolting
More than one reducer or spool piece between manifold and presented flange
Flange face damaged or corroded, or repaired item not retested
say: Our procedure covers correct use, certification, storage with protected flange faces, regular inspection and annual pressure testing. We have an inventory, and each item has a certificate and is marked with the last test date and pressure. Only one reducer is fitted between the manifold and the connection.

practice.q: How often must reducers be pressure tested?
a: At least annually
To 100 percent MAWP
Marked with date and pressure

practice.q: What rating must a reducer have?
a: Same or higher than the fixed manifold piping
Certified with test certificate
Not more than one between flanges

tip: Check the paint marks and flange covers on stored reducers before the inspector does. A new test mark is the easiest evidence.

title: Inert gas system P/V breaking devices
plain: Do officers know the purpose, operation and maintenance of the P/V breaker in the IG main, and is it in good condition?
why: The breaker stops tanks having too much pressure or vacuum if the IG system fails or venting is misused.
checks: Company procedure covering the P/V breaking devices
Marking on the breaker: pressure and vacuum settings, last inspection date, anti-freeze type and lowest temperature
Fabric condition and flame screens
Liquid level and clear, readable level gauge
Your knowledge of purpose and how to check liquid level
ready: Procedure covering inspection, testing and maintenance of the breaker
Inspection and maintenance records with defects
Correct liquid and anti-freeze, at the right level
Flame screens with correct mesh, undamaged
Setting that is higher than secondary venting and within tank structure limits
traps: No procedure including the P/V breaking devices
Poor fabric condition of the breaker
Flame screens damaged, missing, gapped or repaired with wrong mesh
Liquid level not at design setting, or gauge not readable
Breaker not marked with settings, inspection date, anti-freeze details
Breaker set lower than the secondary venting, or outside safe tank limits
Officer cannot explain purpose or how to verify liquid level
say: The P/V breaker protects the tanks from over pressure and vacuum if the IG fails or venting is misused. It is marked with its settings, last inspection date and anti-freeze details, and the liquid level is correct. It is set higher than our secondary venting and within tank design limits.

practice.q: What is the P/V breaker for?
a: Prevent excess pressure in the tanks
Prevent excess vacuum if IG blowers fail
Backup if venting is misused

practice.q: How do you check the liquid level?
a: Read the clear level gauge
Know the correct liquid density
Level may be verifiable only at atmospheric pressure

tip: Learn how your ship's gauge reads when the IG is pressurised versus at atmosphere, because the inspector may ask.

title: Indicators and alarms for the inert gas system
plain: Do officers know the purpose, operation and testing of the IG indicators and alarms, and have they been tested and calibrated correctly?
why: The IG indicators and alarms tell you when the gas is bad or pressure is lost, before air gets into the tanks.
checks: Company procedure covering testing and calibration of IG indicators and alarms
Control panel recorders showing oxygen and main line pressure against date and time
Lamp and alarm test used to prove lamps and alarms work
Local and remote readings consistent: cargo control room, engine room, bridge, deck
Test and calibration records for instruments and alarms
ready: Procedure with test and calibration method, frequency and action on failure
Manufacturer's manuals for all instruments and alarms
Test and calibration records
IG plant inspection and maintenance record with defects and fixes
Calibration facilities and clear instructions at the instruments
traps: Pressure or oxygen indicator or recorder defective, or not matching local readings
Bridge pressure indicator not working or not matching the control panel
Engine room oxygen indicator not working or not matching the analyser
Required audible and visual alarms not working
Independent low-low pressure alarm or pump shutdown not working
No calibration records, facilities or clear instructions
Instruments not in a consistent system of units
say: Our procedure sets how and when we test and calibrate the IG indicators and alarms, and what to do if one fails. I can show the recorders working, run the lamp and alarm test, and show our calibration records. I know the actions for each alarm, such as high oxygen or low pressure.

practice.q: What do you do if the oxygen alarm activates?
a: Follow the company action for the alarm
Stop sending off-spec gas to the tanks
Investigate and record the cause

practice.q: How do you check the indicators agree?
a: Compare local and remote readings
Control room, engine room, bridge and deck
Fix any difference and record it

tip: Run the lamp and alarm test before the inspector arrives so any dead lamps are replaced in advance.

title: Connections and interconnections to the inert gas system
plain: Do officers know the IG connections and interconnections, such as emergency external supply and double-hull connections, and are they in good condition and marked?
why: In an IG failure or when inerting double-hull spaces, the right connections must be ready and safely isolated from the cargo system.
checks: Company procedure covering emergency supply to double-hull spaces, external IG supply and cargo piping link
Connection for external IG supply, clearly marked with its purpose
Portable hoses for double-hull space connection, damaged or missing
Isolation between IG main and cargo piping: spool piece, valves, non-return valve
Your knowledge of the arrangements, including the forepeak where next to cargo
ready: Procedure for the three arrangements as fitted
Detailed IG instruction manuals
Cargo and IG operation log books
Inspection and maintenance records for connections and the non-return valve
Hoses and blanks stored, labelled and in good order
traps: No procedure covering all fitted arrangements
External IG connection not marked with its purpose
Spool piece left in place between IG main and cargo piping
No evidence of inspecting the non-return valve between IG main and cargo piping
Portable hoses damaged or missing
Officer does not know the double-hull or external supply arrangements
say: Our procedure covers emergency IG supply to the double-hull spaces, the external IG supply connection, and the link to the cargo piping where fitted. The external connection is marked, the hoses are in good order, and the non-return valve has been inspected. I know what we do if the IG fails.

practice.q: What do you do if the IG system fails completely?
a: Stop all cargo tank operations
Close the deck isolating valve and open the vent between it and the regulating valve
Repair quickly, use external IG supply if needed to keep tanks inert

practice.q: Which spaces need an IG connection?
a: Double-hull ballast tanks and void spaces next to cargo tanks
Includes forepeak where next to cargo
Not the cargo or ballast pump rooms

tip: Find the external IG flange and the portable hoses on deck and check the labels before the inspection day.

title: Cargo heating system
plain: Do officers know the company procedure for cargo heating, and is the heating system in good condition, tested and used as the procedure says?
why: Wrong heating can damage tank coatings and structure, or let heating medium and cargo mix and contaminate each other.
checks: Company procedure for operation, testing and maintenance of heating, specific to ship and cargo
Coil manifolds, deck heat exchangers, pipework, observation tank or hot well
Records of heating, daily cargo temperatures and system testing
Remote temperature indication and alarms
Your knowledge of cargo temperature limits
ready: Procedure covering testing, return monitoring, pressure, blanking, temperature checks and alarms
Operation manuals for the heating system
Heating usage records and daily temperature records
Records of regular monitoring of system return for leaks
Cargo temperature limits set by operator, class or coating maker
traps: No procedure or no testing and heating records
Heating not isolated or blanked where the procedure requires
No records of regular return checks, or oil layer in the hot well
Leaks of heating medium on deck or in the engine room
Defective temperature sensors
Cargo temperature limits exceeded in the records
Heavy corrosion, soft patches or temporary repairs on heating pipework
say: Our procedure for this ship and cargo covers testing the heating, checking the system return for leaks, keeping the right pressure, blanking coils when needed and watching temperature limits. I can show heating and temperature records, and the observation tank is clean. Temperature alarms are tested.

practice.q: How do you know if a steam heating coil is leaking?
a: Check the observation tank or hot well
A layer of oil on the surface is a problem
Very small traces can be normal

practice.q: When do you blank the heating coils?
a: Cargo must not get excess heat
Heating or cooling medium incompatible with cargo
As the company procedure says

tip: Record every check of the hot well or observation tank during a heated cargo, as the procedure requires. A gap in the record is easy for the inspector to spot.

title: Cargo doping and additives
plain: Do officers know the company procedure for onboard doping, and did they follow it?
why: Adding additives by hand can expose people to toxic or flammable hazards and create static risk if not planned and controlled.
checks: Company procedure for managing onboard doping operations
Doping plans and risk assessments from current or past operations
Doping method, crew supervision, PPE and anti-static precautions, if one is in progress
Stowage of any additives onboard
Safety data sheets for additives
ready: Procedure covering plan review, risk assessment and supervision
Supplier or contractor doping plan before the operation
Ship's own risk assessment, discussed with ship and terminal people
Safety data sheets near the doping point
Pressure test records for any injection system used
traps: No procedure, or no doping plan received from supplier
No risk assessment based on the doping plan
Plan or risk assessment missing hazards, method, supervision, PPE, clean-up or storage
No evidence it was discussed with everyone involved, including contractors
No safety data sheet available or at the doping point
Open tank lid used when another method was possible, or additives free-falling into non-inerted tanks
PPE not used, or contractors not supervised by ship's crew
say: Our procedure requires us to review the doping plan, do a risk assessment and supervise the operation. We prefer shore or in-line injection, and open tank lid only in exceptional cases. The safety data sheet is kept at the doping point and the plan is discussed with everyone involved.

practice.q: What must the doping plan and risk assessment cover?
a: Flammable or toxic hazards, method, supervision
PPE and handling equipment, spill clean-up
Storage and anti-static precautions if not inerted

practice.q: What is the preferred way of doping?
a: Ashore or by in-line injection
Or through the tank vapour locks
Open tank lid only in exceptional cases

tip: Keep a blank doping risk assessment form ready, so you can start it the moment the supplier's plan arrives.

title: Cargo tank temperature monitoring systems
plain: Do officers know the procedures for maintaining, testing and calibrating cargo temperature monitoring equipment, and is it in good condition?
why: Temperature readings protect tank coatings and structure and are needed to calculate the cargo quantity.
checks: Company procedure for maintenance, testing and calibration
Demonstration of fixed temperature monitoring equipment and alarms
Manufacturer's manuals and instructions
Records of checks, tests and calibration
Portable temperature equipment serviced and calibrated
ready: Procedure following manufacturer's instructions, maybe in planned maintenance
Manufacturer's manuals for the fixed system
Calibration records, fixed system within the last 30 months
Calibration certificates for portable instruments
Cross-check of fixed against portable readings
traps: No procedure or no records of checks, tests or calibration
Officer cannot demonstrate the fixed equipment and alarms
Fixed equipment not calibrated within the last 30 months
Not tested and calibrated to manufacturer's instructions, fixed or portable
One or more temperature sensors defective
Visible or audible alarm defective
say: Our procedure covers maintenance, testing and calibration to the manufacturer's instructions. I can show the fixed system and its alarms working. Calibration of the fixed system has been done within 30 months and the records are here. We also compare portable and fixed readings as a cross-check.

practice.q: How often is the fixed temperature system calibrated?
a: Per manufacturer's instructions
Preferably not more than 30 months apart
Often done during repair periods

practice.q: How do you check a fixed sensor between calibrations?
a: Compare against a portable instrument
Record the comparison
Report any sensor that disagrees

tip: Put the next calibration due date for the fixed system on the planned maintenance calendar so it is never missed.

title: Cargo manifold arrangements
plain: Do officers know the company procedures for managing cargo and vapour connections at the manifolds, and are the manifolds in good condition?
why: Poorly made-up or unblanked manifold connections are a common source of spills and leaks.
checks: Company procedure for managing cargo and vapour connections at manifolds
Manifold connections: full bolting, hose or arm support, pressure gauges
Blanks on unused connections, drains and sample points
Drip trays: present, clean and drained, no covers over gratings
Bow and stern manifolds, vapour manifold keying and marking, platform edge protection
ready: Procedure covering connections, gauges, blanks, drip trays, vapour manifolds, platforms, hose support, crane use, bow and stern manifolds
Documentation for blank flange pressure rating where blanks are not the same thickness
Clean drip trays with working drains, valves capped
Pressure gauge on each connection outboard of the valve, with valve and cap when not fitted
Spray guards for acids or toxic or corrosive cargo on chemical ships
traps: Bolts damaged or wrong size, or not a bolt in every hole
Improvised G-clamp or camlocks not fully engaged
Loading arm supported on items not meant to carry load
Cargo hose not properly supported
Unused manifold not blanked, or leaking, or drain or sample point not capped
No drip tray, dirty drip trays, plastic trays not bonded, or manifolds drained into open trays
Midships crane used for stores during cargo, or edge protection missing on high platform
Stern manifold not isolated, or three-metre danger area not marked
say: Our procedure covers hose or arm connections, pressure gauges, blanks on all unused connections, drains and sample points, drip trays, vapour manifolds and safe work on the platform. Every flange has a bolt in every hole, and drip trays are clean and drained. Unused lines are blanked, not just closed by valves.

practice.q: Why blank unused manifolds instead of relying on the valve?
a: Valve tightness cannot be relied on
Prevents leaks and seepage
Blanks fully bolted and rated for the line

practice.q: How do you avoid mixing up vapour and liquid connections?
a: Keyed flange with a stud at 12 o'clock
Vapour connections painted or marked
Check at pre-transfer

tip: Walk the manifold with the bosun before each cargo and check bolts, blanks, drip trays and gauges as a fixed routine.

title: Receiving nitrogen from shore
plain: Do officers know the company procedure for receiving shore nitrogen to inert, purge, pad tanks or clear lines?
why: Shore nitrogen can come at high pressure and flow, and can over-pressurise and damage cargo tanks very quickly.
checks: Company procedure for receiving nitrogen from shore
Risk assessments and records from at least one operation in the last six months
Ship shore safety checklist showing agreed procedure, maximum pressure and flow rate
Your knowledge of how the incoming flow is controlled
Whether flammable-cargo lines were cleared to the ship with nitrogen, not compressed air
ready: Procedure covering risk assessment, connection and piping choice, and flow control
Completed risk assessment for each nitrogen receipt
Completed ship shore checklist items on nitrogen, pressure and flow
Records of the latest operation within six months
Plan to pad through the vapour system where possible
traps: No procedure for receiving nitrogen for inerting, purging, padding or line clearing
Procedure does not cover risk assessment, connection choice or flow control
Risk assessment not available for a past nitrogen receipt
Checklist did not record agreed pressure and flow rate
Hoses or arms with flammable cargo cleared to the ship using compressed air
Officer unfamiliar with the procedure
say: Before we take nitrogen from shore we carry out a risk assessment and agree the pressure and flow rate with the terminal on the checklist. We control the incoming flow so it never exceeds what our vents can pass. We pad through the vapour system where possible and never clear flammable lines with compressed air.

practice.q: What is the main danger of shore nitrogen?
a: High pressure and flow can over-pressurise tanks quickly
Flow may exceed P/V valve capacity
Possible structural damage and loss of containment

practice.q: How do you control the incoming flow?
a: Agree pressure and flow with the terminal
Restrict flow to what vents or vapour return can pass
Do not throttle with the manifold valve; use it only as an emergency stop

tip: Brief the whole watch at the pre-transfer conference on who watches tank pressure and who can stop the flow.

title: Carriage of inhibited cargoes
plain: Do officers know the company procedures for carrying inhibited cargoes, and were they followed?
why: If an inhibited cargo starts to self-react, it can heat up and form solids or explosive peroxides.
checks: Company procedure for carriage of inhibited cargoes
Inhibitor certificate with the minimum required information
Cargo logs, temperature records and inert gas logs
Contingency plan for uncontrolled polymerisation
Your knowledge of the procedure, as cargo planning officer
ready: Procedure covering certificates, temperature checks, inerting, reliquefaction draining, anti-freeze, water, recirculation, adding inhibitor, toxicity, contingency
Inhibitor certificate: name and amount, date added and effective life, temperature limits, action if voyage is longer
Daily temperature records of inhibited cargo
Cargo plans for load and discharge
Oxygen records below 0.1 percent for inert gas on vinyl chloride, where relevant
traps: No procedure covering all required items
No certificate on board, or certificate missing minimum information
Inhibitor effectiveness period expired before discharge
Temperature not checked at least daily, or as the maker advises
No contingency plan for uncontrolled polymerisation and rapid temperature rise
No records that inert gas oxygen was below 0.1 percent where vinyl chloride was protected by inert gas
say: Our procedure covers the inhibitor certificate, temperature monitoring, inerting, purging the reliquefaction system, water exclusion, cargo recirculation and what to do for uncontrolled polymerisation. We would refuse an inhibited cargo without a proper certificate. Temperatures are recorded daily during the voyage.

practice.q: What must the inhibitor certificate tell you?
a: Name and amount of inhibitor
Date added and how long it works
Temperature limits and what to do if voyage is longer

practice.q: What do you do about the reliquefaction system when it is shut down?
a: Drain or purge it with inhibited cargo
Inhibitor may not boil off with the cargo
Prevents self-reaction in the system

tip: If no inhibited cargo was carried in the last six months, be ready to say when the last one was and show that record.

title: Cargo sampling
plain: Do officers know the company procedures for cargo sampling on an LPG ship?
why: Sampling releases cargo near people, so poor equipment or control can lead to exposure, fire or toxic vapour release.
checks: Company procedure for sampling every cargo on the Certificate of Fitness
Sampling equipment and connections for compatibility
Marking of sample connections, and whether they are capped when not in use
Sampling in progress, if any, with responsible officer present
Your knowledge of PPE, equipment, connections and locations
ready: Procedure, possibly in the cargo system operation manual
Compatible equipment with correctly marked connections, double valves on liquid samples
Closed-loop equipment for toxic cargoes
PPE and SCBA for toxic cargoes
Certified safe electrical equipment if used
traps: Sampling with no responsible officer present
Sample equipment not compatible with connections, or badly connected
Open-loop sampling used on a toxic cargo
No double valves on liquid sampling, or neither valve multi-turn
Inerting or gassing-up connections used for cargo sampling
Missing PPE, or no SCBA for toxic cargo
Sample connection not capped, or vapour-contaminated containers stored in an unventilated space
Plastic vapour bags used for liquid samples
say: A responsible officer authorises and directly supervises every sampling job. We use only compatible equipment, minimise venting, purge and ullage containers in a safe place, and use closed-loop equipment with SCBA for toxic cargoes. Connections are marked and capped when not in use.

practice.q: When must closed-loop sampling be used?
a: When sampling toxic products
Open loop may be used for flammable-only cargoes, with release kept to a minimum
Minimise venting always

practice.q: What PPE do you use for sampling?
a: Gloves, goggles and protective clothing for cold cargo
SCBA for toxic cargo
Not just a respirator in an enclosed space

tip: Always check the sample container fits the connection before you start. If it does not, any fix must not affect the gastight integrity of the ship's system.

title: Segregating incompatible cargoes and refrigerants
plain: Do officers know how to spot and separate incompatible cargoes and refrigerants when planning cargo stowage, and was it done?
why: Mixing incompatible cargoes or refrigerants can cause dangerous reactions and contamination.
checks: Company procedure for identifying and segregating incompatible cargoes and refrigerants
Compatibility chart from a recognised body, and data used
Current and previous cargo stowage plans
Spool pieces, spectacle flanges or blanks as shown in the stowage plan
Your knowledge of the chart and procedure, as the stowage planner
ready: Procedure covering how to identify, document and achieve segregation
Recognised compatibility chart and safety data sheets
Stowage plans that show where care is needed, which cargoes and the segregation method
Cargo log entries of pipeline isolation before incompatible loading
Segregation drawings in the cargo system operation manual
traps: No procedure covering identification, documentation and means of segregation
Officer unfamiliar with the procedure or the chart
No compatibility chart from a recognised body onboard
Incompatible cargoes stowed next to each other without positive segregation
Segregation fitted on the ship not as shown in the stowage plan
Stowage plan not showing when and where to avoid mixing
No cargo log entry of isolating pipelines before loading incompatible cargoes
say: Our procedure uses the charterer's instructions, the compatibility chart and shipper's data to identify incompatible cargoes and refrigerants. The stowage plan shows which cargoes are involved and how we segregate them, using spool pieces or blanks. The isolation is logged, and if in doubt we treat cargoes as incompatible.

practice.q: What do you do if you are unsure two cargoes are compatible?
a: Check data sheets and compatibility chart
Seek advice from shippers
If still unclear, treat as incompatible and use positive segregation

practice.q: What is positive segregation?
a: Removable spool pieces or pipe sections
Applies to liquid, vapour and vent lines
Record the isolation in the cargo log

tip: Walk the plan on deck: confirm every spool piece and blank shown on paper is actually fitted or removed.

title: Carriage of propylene oxide and ethylene oxide
plain: Do officers know the company procedures for safely carrying propylene oxide, ethylene oxide and PO-EO mixtures?
why: These cargoes are flammable, toxic and self-reactive, so mistakes can lead to fire, explosion or serious exposure.
checks: Company procedure, approved cargo handling plans and the P&A Manual
If carried in the last 12 months: segregation certificate, last three cargoes, tank inspection and cleaning records
Records of tank pressure, oxygen, and hold space monitoring
If loaded now: seals on pipeline blanks, and water spray system ready
Your knowledge of the procedure topics
ready: Procedure covering tank preparation, separation of pipelines and compressors, relief valve settings, nitrogen, discharge, vapour return, temperature, hold spaces, sampling, emergencies
Certificate of Fitness or NLS certificate listing these cargoes
Segregation certificate issued by the shore authority before loading
Records of the last three cargoes before PO or EO
Jettison equipment and water spray system in working order
traps: No procedure, or officer unfamiliar with the topics
Cargo not on the Certificate of Fitness or NLS certificate, no approved handling plan or no P&A Manual
No segregation certificate before loading
Ethylene oxide carried in deck tanks
Pipeline blanks not sealed while handling
Tank pressure not kept above 0.007 MPa gauge during discharge
Hoses not marked 'for alkylene oxide transfer only'
No hold space monitoring records, hold oxygen over 2 percent where inerting required
Water spray not working, no jettison equipment, no cooling system where required
say: Our procedure covers tank preparation and compatibility with previous cargoes, separation of pipelines and compressors, nitrogen padding, pressure settings, discharge, vapour return, temperature control, hold space monitoring, sampling and emergencies. We have the segregation certificate, the P&A Manual and approved handling plans, and the water spray system is ready.

practice.q: Why are PO and EO carried under nitrogen?
a: They are self-reactive, especially with air
Cannot be inhibited, so inert gas used
Keep a positive pressure and low oxygen

practice.q: What documents must be on board for these cargoes?
a: Certificate of Fitness or NLS certificate listing them
Approved cargo handling plan
P&A Manual and segregation certificate

tip: If your ship is not certified for PO or EO, tell the inspector at the start so the question can be marked not applicable.

title: Escape sets required by the IGC Code
plain: Are there enough escape sets for everyone on board, giving proper breathing and eye protection?
why: In a toxic gas leak, every person needs a set to get out of the hazardous area safely.
checks: Inspection and maintenance records for escape sets in the maintenance plan
Two escape sets picked at random and inspected
Number of sets against everyone on board while underway, including visitors and contractors
Marking: not for fire-fighting or cargo handling
Rating's knowledge of location, purpose and operation
ready: Sets for every person, in addition to the SOLAS EEBDs in accommodation and machinery spaces
Duration of at least 15 minutes, no filter-type sets, eye protection included
Sets fully charged and marked not for fire-fighting or cargo handling
Company procedure covering use and maintenance
Maintenance records within the planned maintenance system
traps: Set duration under 15 minutes, or filter-type protection
No suitable eye protection
Not marked as not for fire-fighting or cargo handling
Not in addition to the SOLAS EEBDs, or not in the procedures and maintenance plan
Set not fully charged, or not inspected as the plan says
Set used for fire-fighting, cargo handling or as the main way to enter unsafe spaces
Too few sets for everyone including contractors and visitors
Rating does not know where sets are or how to use them
say: We carry escape sets for everyone on board, in addition to the SOLAS EEBDs. They give at least 15 minutes, include eye protection, and are marked not for fire-fighting or cargo handling. They are in our maintenance plan, and I can show the records.

practice.q: Can you use an escape set to enter a tank space?
a: No, escape only
Not the main way to enter unsafe atmospheres
Not for fire-fighting or cargo handling

practice.q: How many sets do you need?
a: One for every person on board while underway
Include contractors and visitors
In addition to SOLAS EEBDs

tip: Update the headcount for the sets whenever supernumeraries or contractors join, so the number never falls short.

title: Cargo tank insulation
plain: Do officers know the company procedure for inspecting and maintaining cargo tank insulation, and is the insulation reported as in good condition?
why: Insulation limits heat getting into the cargo and protects the hull steel from cold damage.
checks: Company procedure for inspection and maintenance of tank insulation
Records of inspection, maintenance and repair
Defect reports for any defects found in inspections
Enclosed space entry records for recent insulation inspections
Your knowledge of the procedure
ready: Procedure covering scope, frequency, maintenance, records and fire safety near insulation
Inspection and repair records, maybe within the maintenance plan or hold space inspections
Open defect reports with follow-up action
Enclosed space entry permits for inspections
Hot work precautions covering gas in insulation
traps: No procedure covering scope and frequency, maintenance, records and fire safety
Officer unfamiliar with the procedure
No inspection, maintenance or repair records
Inspections not done as the procedure says
Defect noted in an inspection but no defect report raised
say: Our procedure covers the scope and frequency of insulation inspections, maintenance, records, and fire precautions for any work near the insulation. Inspections are done with enclosed space entry permits and recorded. Any defects found get a defect report for follow-up.

practice.q: What do you check for during an insulation inspection?
a: Condition of insulation and vapour barrier
Signs of moisture or damage
Record defects and raise a defect report

practice.q: What fire precautions apply when hot work is near insulation?
a: Check area for gas in the insulation
Cover exposed insulation with non-flammable material
Insulation may be combustible

tip: Link the insulation inspection to your hold space inspection routine so it is never missed.

title: Vent outlet protection screens or flame screens
plain: Are the cargo vent outlets fitted with the right protection screen or flame screen for the cargo, and are they in good condition?
why: Some cargoes need flame screens to stop a vent mast fire or lightning strike reaching the tank, and a blocked screen can raise tank pressure.
checks: Cargo records or maintenance plans showing correct screen for the cargo carried
Condition of screens on vent outlets: not blocked, painted or damaged
Storage of any flame screens not in use
Flame screens available on board if the ship has an NLS certificate
Carbon dioxide cargo: no screens fitted
ready: Protection screens up to 13 mm square mesh for gas cargoes in general
Flame screens or safety heads for the listed NLS cargoes
Flame screens stored safely and clearly marked so they can be found
Maintenance records showing inspection of screens
Cargo plan showing which screen suits the cargo
traps: Wrong or no screen fitted for the cargo
Screen blocked, clogged, painted over or damaged
Flame screens not in use stored badly or not marked
NLS certificate on ship but no flame screens available onboard
Screens fitted on vent outlets while carrying carbon dioxide
say: Our cargo plan shows which screen goes on the vent outlets for each cargo. Flame screens go on for the listed NLS cargoes and the coarse protection screens are used otherwise. We never paint screens, and unused flame screens are stored and marked so they are easy to find.

practice.q: Which screen do you fit for normal LPG cargoes?
a: Protection screen, not more than 13 mm square mesh
Stops foreign objects entering
Must not hinder vent flow

practice.q: What is different for carbon dioxide?
a: No flame screens or protection screens on vent outlets
Cargo may solidify and block
Follow the IGC Code requirement

tip: Before loading an NLS cargo, check the flame screens are actually onboard and fit the mast, not just listed.

title: Custody transfer measurement system (CTMS)
plain: Do officers know the company procedures for operating, testing and calibrating the CTMS, and is the system in good condition?
why: The CTMS gives the official cargo quantity, which is used for sale and tax, so errors are costly.
checks: Company procedure for operation, testing and calibration
Manufacturer's manuals
Records of pre-operational tests and service and calibration records
Current calibration certificate onboard
Your knowledge of the procedure
ready: Procedure covering pre-arrival checks, servicing and periodic calibration
Manufacturer's manuals and instructions
Pre-operational test record for this loading or discharge
Current calibration certificate
Service and calibration records
traps: No procedure for operation, testing and calibration
Not calibrated as the procedure requires
No current calibration certificate onboard
No records of pre-operational tests, or no test before the current operation
System defective in any way
say: Our procedure covers pre-arrival checks, servicing and periodic calibration of the CTMS. The calibration certificate is current, and we test the system before each loading or discharge and record it. I can show the manuals and records.

practice.q: What does the CTMS do?
a: Takes level, temperature, pressure, trim and list readings
Calculates volume and average temperatures
Gives the official record of quantity transferred

practice.q: When is the CTMS calibrated?
a: As the company procedure requires
Commonly at each drydocking
In-service verification can be done at mid-cycle

tip: Keep the latest calibration certificate in the cargo control room folder so you can hand it over at once.

title: Gas combustion unit (GCU)
plain: Do officers know the company procedures for operating, inspecting, maintaining and testing the GCU?
why: The GCU burns excess boil-off gas safely, so venting methane is avoided and tank pressure stays under control.
checks: Company procedure for operation, inspection, maintenance and testing of the GCU
Records of inspection, maintenance and testing, including alarms
GCU and its equipment in the engine room
Your knowledge of failure actions, manual gas isolation and alarm tests
Space ventilation, gas and fire detection, and flame screens on vents or bleed lines
ready: Procedure covering who supervises, hazards, controls, failure in auto mode and manual operation
Test records for alarms: flame failure, combustion air, cooling air, BOG inlet temperature, exit temperature, methane in duct, duct ventilation or nitrogen pressure
Records of inspection and maintenance in the maintenance plan
Manual gas fuel isolation from a safe accessible position
Working ventilation, gas detection and fire detection in the GCU space
traps: No procedure for the GCU
Officer unfamiliar with failure in automatic mode and manual operation
Officer unaware of manual gas isolation position
Officer unfamiliar with GCU alarm tests
Inspections, tests or maintenance not done as required
Defective GCU, space ventilation, gas detection or fire detection
Vents or bleed lines that may hold gas fuel not fitted with flame screens
say: Our procedure says who supervises the GCU, the hazards and how we control them, and what we do if automatic mode fails, including manual operation. We test the alarms, such as flame failure and high exit temperature at 535 degrees C, and keep the records. I can show the manual gas isolation point.

practice.q: Why do you have a GCU?
a: Burn excess boil-off gas safely
Avoid venting methane
Handles gas when it cannot be used as fuel or reliquefied

practice.q: What alarms do you test on the GCU?
a: Flame failure, loss of combustion or cooling air
BOG inlet and exit gas temperature, high-high at 535 degrees C
Methane in gas duct, duct ventilation or nitrogen pressure

tip: Make sure the GCU is left in automatic mode, as the guidance expects, and know how to take over manually.
